claim: Planarian ptk7 is expressed in an animal-wide graded fashion maximally in the trunk, and also the CNS and pharynx.
source: We examined PCGs as defined by prior homology and expression profiling studies (Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Reddien, 2011; Witchley et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2015; Reuter et al., 2015) and found a unique expression pattern for a planarian homolog of ptk7, expressed in an animal-wide graded fashion maximally in the trunk, and also the CNS and pharynx (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and expression pattern analysis.

claim: Planarian ptk7 is expressed in collagen+ cells of the body-wall musculature.
source: Like other described PCGs, planarian ptk7 was expressed in collagen+ cells of the body-wall musculature (Witchley et al., 2013) and aspects of its expression domain could become re-established after amputation even in irradiated animals lacking neoblasts and the ability to form new tissues (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by double FISH showing coexpression with collagen marker and citation to prior work on PCG expression patterns.

claim: ptk7 expression can be re-established after amputation even in irradiated animals lacking neoblasts.
source: Like other described PCGs, planarian ptk7 was expressed in collagen+ cells of the body-wall musculature (Witchley et al., 2013) and aspects of its expression domain could become re-established after amputation even in irradiated animals lacking neoblasts and the ability to form new tissues (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in irradiated animals shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: ptk7(RNAi) animals regenerating from trunk fragments form an ectopic posterior mouth at 83% penetrance.
source: In ptk7(RNAi) animals amputated to remove both head and tail, regeneration produced a normal head and tail (35/35) but caused formation of an ectopic posterior mouth at a high penetrance (83%, n=35) and, more rarely, formation of an ectopic posterior pharynx with broadly normal orientation with respect to the primary body axis (14%, n=35) (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis and imaging data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: ptk7(RNAi) animals regenerating from trunk fragments form an ectopic posterior pharynx at 14% penetrance.
source: In ptk7(RNAi) animals amputated to remove both head and tail, regeneration produced a normal head and tail (35/35) but caused formation of an ectopic posterior mouth at a high penetrance (83%, n=35) and, more rarely, formation of an ectopic posterior pharynx with broadly normal orientation with respect to the primary body axis (14%, n=35) (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis and imaging data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: ptk7 limits trunk identity in planarian regeneration.
source: Thus, ptk7 limits trunk identity in planarian regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the ectopic trunk structures (mouth and pharynx) formed upon ptk7 inhibition.

claim: Co-inhibition of ptk7 with wntP-2 causes 100% penetrance of ectopic pharynx phenotype.
source: Co-inhibition of ptk7 with either wntP-2/wnt11-5/wnt4b (hereafter referred to as wntP-2), ndl-3, Dvl-2 (Almuedo-Castillo et al., 2011), or fzd-1/2/7 caused the strongest enhancement of the ectopic pharynx phenotype, resulting in 100% of animals affected, whereas co-inhibition with other PCGs affected this phenotype more weakly and below statistical significance under these conditions.
evidence: Supported by RNAi enhancement screen data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: wntP-2 encodes a Wnt gene expressed in a graded fashion from the posterior.
source: wntP-2 encodes a Wnt gene expressed in a graded fashion from the posterior (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and based on phylogenetic analyses has been proposed to be either a Wnt11 (Gurley et al., 2010) or Wnt4 (Riddiford and Olson, 2011) family member.
evidence: Supported by expression pattern data and citations to phylogenetic analyses.

claim: ndl-3 encodes a member of the conserved FGFRL/nou-darake class of cell-surface molecules that lacks a tyrosine kinase intracellular domain.
source: Planarian ndl-3 is expressed in a graded fashion from the anterior (Rink et al., 2009) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and encodes a member of the conserved FGFRL/nou-darake class of cell-surface molecules that possess an FGF-receptor-like extracellular domain but lacks a tyrosine kinase intracellular domain and are thus proposed to function as FGF signaling inhibitors (Cebrià et al., 2002; Gerber et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by sequence homology analysis and citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: ndl-3 is expressed in a graded fashion from the anterior.
source: Planarian ndl-3 is expressed in a graded fashion from the anterior (Rink et al., 2009) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and encodes a member of the conserved FGFRL/nou-darake class of cell-surface molecules that possess an FGF-receptor-like extracellular domain but lacks a tyrosine kinase intracellular domain and are thus proposed to function as FGF signaling inhibitors (Cebrià et al., 2002; Gerber et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by expression pattern data and citation to prior work.

claim: Individual inhibition of ptk7 causes ectopic posterior mouths in 86% of regenerating trunk fragments.
source: Individual inhibition of ptk7, wntP-2, and ndl-3 caused formation of ectopic posterior mouths (30/35 ptk7(RNAi) animals, 22/33 wntP-2(RNAi) animals, 14/23 ndl-3(RNAi) animals), and ectopic posterior pharynges (5/35 ptk7(RNAi) animals, 8/33 wntP-2(RNAi) animals, 2/23 ndl-3(RNAi) animals) in amputated animals regenerating both their heads and tails compared to controls (0/46 animals) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Individual inhibition of wntP-2 causes ectopic posterior mouths in 67% of regenerating trunk fragments.
source: Individual inhibition of ptk7, wntP-2, and ndl-3 caused formation of ectopic posterior mouths (30/35 ptk7(RNAi) animals, 22/33 wntP-2(RNAi) animals, 14/23 ndl-3(RNAi) animals), and ectopic posterior pharynges (5/35 ptk7(RNAi) animals, 8/33 wntP-2(RNAi) animals, 2/23 ndl-3(RNAi) animals) in amputated animals regenerating both their heads and tails compared to controls (0/46 animals) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Individual inhibition of ndl-3 causes ectopic posterior mouths in 61% of regenerating trunk fragments.
source: Individual inhibition of ptk7, wntP-2, and ndl-3 caused formation of ectopic posterior mouths (30/35 ptk7(RNAi) animals, 22/33 wntP-2(RNAi) animals, 14/23 ndl-3(RNAi) animals), and ectopic posterior pharynges (5/35 ptk7(RNAi) animals, 8/33 wntP-2(RNAi) animals, 2/23 ndl-3(RNAi) animals) in amputated animals regenerating both their heads and tails compared to controls (0/46 animals) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Pairwise co-inhibition of ptk7, wntP-2, and ndl-3 enhances trunk expansion phenotypes compared to single inhibition.
source: Inhibition of any pairwise combinations of the three genes enhanced the trunk expansion phenotypes (Figure 2A–B) (animals with ectopic pharynges: 45/55 wntP-2(RNAi);ptk7(RNAi), 29/32 ptk7(RNAi);ndl-3(RNAi), 24/40 wntP-2(RNAi);ndl-3(RNAi)), with double-RNAi animals also frequently forming two ectopic pharynges (Figure 2A) and co-inhibition of ptk7 and wntP-2 producing highest penetrance and expressivity of trunk duplication phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis comparing single and double RNAi conditions.

claim: The ectopic pharynx in ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) animals is functional and can obtain food.
source: Live animals with ectopic pharynges were observed during feeding, and the duplicated pharynx could obtain food (Figure 2D, Video 1), suggesting normal functionality of this organ.
evidence: Supported by live imaging observations shown in Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: Prolonged co-inhibition of wntP-2 and ptk7 in uninjured animals causes formation of an ectopic pharynx.
source: Prolonged co-inhibition of wntP-2 and ptk7 produced animals with an ectopic pharynx, indicating that these genes together restrict trunk identity homeostatically in the absence of injury (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis in uninjured animals shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ptk7, wntP-2, and ndl-3 suppress trunk expansion in a context-dependent manner.
source: However, these results indicate that ptk7, wntP-2 and ndl-3 suppress trunk expansion in a context-dependent manner and suggest they may provide information about trunk absence or presence during regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that head and tail fragments do not show ectopic pharynx formation under the same RNAi conditions that cause it in trunk fragments.

claim: ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) regenerating trunk fragments have normal anterior pole and brain regions.
source: Such ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) or ptk7(RNAi);ndl-3(RNAi) regenerating animals had normal anterior pole and brain regions (marked by notum, ndk) and a normal pre-pharyngeal region anterior to the original pharynx (marked by wnt2 and novel gene SMU15014980), expansion of trunk-related peripharyngeal cells (expressing mmp1, FoxA, and SMU15007112), a reduced domain of PCGs expressed in the posterior (wnt11-1, fzd-4-1 and Abd-Ba), and normal expression of wnt1 at the posterior pole.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis of regional markers shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) regenerating trunk fragments show expansion of trunk-related peripharyngeal cells.
source: Such ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) or ptk7(RNAi);ndl-3(RNAi) regenerating animals had normal anterior pole and brain regions (marked by notum, ndk) and a normal pre-pharyngeal region anterior to the original pharynx (marked by wnt2 and novel gene SMU15014980), expansion of trunk-related peripharyngeal cells (expressing mmp1, FoxA, and SMU15007112), a reduced domain of PCGs expressed in the posterior (wnt11-1, fzd-4-1 and Abd-Ba), and normal expression of wnt1 at the posterior pole.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis showing increased expression domains of trunk markers.

claim: ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) regenerating trunk fragments show a reduced domain of posterior PCGs.
source: Such ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) or ptk7(RNAi);ndl-3(RNAi) regenerating animals had normal anterior pole and brain regions (marked by notum, ndk) and a normal pre-pharyngeal region anterior to the original pharynx (marked by wnt2 and novel gene SMU15014980), expansion of trunk-related peripharyngeal cells (expressing mmp1, FoxA, and SMU15007112), a reduced domain of PCGs expressed in the posterior (wnt11-1, fzd-4-1 and Abd-Ba), and normal expression of wnt1 at the posterior pole.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis showing decreased expression domains of tail markers.

claim: Both the pre-existing and ectopic pharynx in wntP-2(RNAi);ptk7(RNAi) animals can regenerate after amputation.
source: Both the pre-existing and ectopic pharynx were capable of regeneration after amputation by sodium azide treatment (Adler et al., 2014), suggesting that wntP-2/ptk7 signaling acts in part to limit the size of the trunk region within the posterior rather than only functioning to position the anterior extent of newly made trunk tissue (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by chemical amputation and regeneration experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) sexual strain animals form both an ectopic pharynx and ectopic reproductive organs.
source: We next inhibited ptk7 and wntP-2 in a regenerating sexual strain of S. mediterranea that forms reproductive organs posterior to the pharynx upon attainment of appropriate size. Such animals formed both an ectopic pharynx and ectopic reproductive organs marked by laminin and dmd-1 expression respectively (Chong et al., 2013), indicating ptk7 and wntP-2 regulate trunk regionalization beyond only control of pharynx and mouth formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by marker expression analysis in sexual strain animals shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) animals form ectopic FoxA+ cells by day 7 of regeneration.
source: Indeed, ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) animals regenerating an ectopic pharynx produced an ectopic domain of FoxA+ cells at a time (7 days of regeneration) prior to appearance of a fully formed ectopic pharynx (14 days of regeneration) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by FoxA expression analysis at different time points shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ndl-3, ptk7, and wntP-2 are expressed in overlapping domains along the anteroposterior axis.
source: Visual inspection of colorimetric in situ hybridizations suggested that ndl-3, ptk7, and wntP-2 are expressed in overlapping domains along the anteroposterior axis (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by colorimetric in situ hybridization images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ndl-3 staining intensity is maximal in the anterior in a region of graded ptk7 staining.
source: ndl-3 staining intensity was maximal in the anterior in a region of graded ptk7 staining. ptk7 staining was maximal in the trunk region in which wntP-2 and ndl-3 staining form opposing gradients. wntP-2 staining was maximal in the posterior tail in a region of relatively less ptk7 expression.
evidence: Supported by quantification of in situ hybridization staining intensity shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ptk7 staining is maximal in the trunk region where wntP-2 and ndl-3 staining form opposing gradients.
source: ndl-3 staining intensity was maximal in the anterior in a region of graded ptk7 staining. ptk7 staining was maximal in the trunk region in which wntP-2 and ndl-3 staining form opposing gradients. wntP-2 staining was maximal in the posterior tail in a region of relatively less ptk7 expression.
evidence: Supported by quantification of in situ hybridization staining intensity shown in Figure 4B.

claim: wntP-2 staining is maximal in the posterior tail in a region of relatively less ptk7 expression.
source: ndl-3 staining intensity was maximal in the anterior in a region of graded ptk7 staining. ptk7 staining was maximal in the trunk region in which wntP-2 and ndl-3 staining form opposing gradients. wntP-2 staining was maximal in the posterior tail in a region of relatively less ptk7 expression.
evidence: Supported by quantification of in situ hybridization staining intensity shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cells co-expressing wntP-2 and ndl-3 exist in head-to-trunk proximal regions.
source: This approach identified cells that co-express wntP-2 and ndl-3 (in particular in head-to trunk proximal regions R3-R5, Figure 4E), ptk7 and ndl-3 (head-to-trunk regions R2-R4), and ptk7 and wntP-2 (trunk-to-tail regions R5-R7).
evidence: Supported by triple FISH analysis and quantification shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Cells co-expressing ptk7 and ndl-3 exist in head-to-trunk regions.
source: This approach identified cells that co-express wntP-2 and ndl-3 (in particular in head-to trunk proximal regions R3-R5, Figure 4E), ptk7 and ndl-3 (head-to-trunk regions R2-R4), and ptk7 and wntP-2 (trunk-to-tail regions R5-R7).
evidence: Supported by triple FISH analysis and quantification shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Cells co-expressing ptk7 and wntP-2 exist in trunk-to-tail regions.
source: This approach identified cells that co-express wntP-2 and ndl-3 (in particular in head-to trunk proximal regions R3-R5, Figure 4E), ptk7 and ndl-3 (head-to-trunk regions R2-R4), and ptk7 and wntP-2 (trunk-to-tail regions R5-R7).
evidence: Supported by triple FISH analysis and quantification shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: β-catenin-1 inhibition in uninjured animals severely reduces the expression of ptk7, wntP-2 and ndl-3.
source: β-catenin-1 inhibition in uninjured animals severely reduced the expression of ptk7, wntP-2 and ndl-3 (Figure 5A), consistent with prior analyses of their expression requirements in regeneration (Owen et al., 2015; Reuter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis after β-catenin-1 RNAi shown in Figure 5A and citations to prior studies.

claim: APC(RNAi) regenerating animals form an ectopic anterior tail that expresses wntP-2 throughout.
source: Such animals regenerated anterior tails that expressed wntP-2 throughout, that expressed ptk7 strongly in a region near the amputation plane and away from the terminus, and that lacked ndl-3 expression.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis in APC(RNAi) animals shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-inhibition of ptk7 and wntP-2 or ptk7 and ndl-3 has no detectable effect on expression of β-catenin-dependent transcripts axin-B and teashirt.
source: However, co-inhibition of ptk7 and wntP-2 or ptk7 and ndl-3 had no detectable effect on expression of beta-catenin-dependent transcripts axin-B and teashirt (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–B) (Owen et al., 2015; Reuter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: Co-inhibition of ptk7/wntP-2 with APC does not enhance or suppress ectopic pharynx formation.
source: We could not detect any enhancement or suppression of ectopic pharynx formation in that assay, further suggesting independence between ptk7/wntP-2 and APC/β-catenin-1 signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis of triple RNAi shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Trunk regionalization can be separable from pole identity.
source: These observations argue for a specific regulatory relationship in which ptk7 and wntP-2 together suppress expression of ndl-3 in the posterior. Alternatively, the nascent pharynx could exert influence over the expression of ndl-3 in a manner indirectly controlled by ptk7 and wntP-2's suppression of pharynx identity. Together these experiments indicate ptk7, wntP-2 and ndl-3 can directly or indirectly engage in regulatory interactions in homeostatic maintenance of tissue pattern and also in re-establishment of pattern in regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the distinct phenotypes of β-catenin-1 RNAi (ectopic head) versus ptk7/wntP-2 RNAi (ectopic trunk without affecting poles).

claim: In regenerating tail fragments, pharynx formation coincides with early reduction of wntP-2 expression and increase in ndl-3 expression.
source: Notably, the position of the newly regenerated pharynx correlated with a domain in which wntP-2 expression was reduced and ndl-3 was elevated.
evidence: Supported by time-course expression analysis in regenerating tail fragments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In tail fragments, inhibition of ptk7 causes a posterior shift to the location of the mouth and pharynx.
source: In tail fragments, inhibition of ptk7 caused a posterior shift to the location of the mouth and pharynx (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), an effect enhanced by co-inhibition of wntP-2 or ndl-3 though not caused by wntP-2 or ndl-3 inhibition alone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of pharynx position shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reduced doses of wntP-2 and ptk7 dsRNA result in intermediate pharynx placement phenotypes.
source: Reduced doses of wntP-2 and ptk7 dsRNA resulted in intermediate placement phenotypes, and the distributions of placement phenotypes were not biphasic (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), suggesting the activity of these genes could regulate pharynx position in a graded fashion rather than controlling a switch between two alternate organ locations.
evidence: Supported by dose-response analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ptk7 acts before day 3 of regeneration in tail fragments.
source: RNAi of ptk7 for three days prior to tail amputation resulted in a posterior shift in the location of the newly formed laminin expression domain detected as early as 3 days of regeneration (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A). These results indicate that ptk7 acts before day 3 of regeneration.
evidence: Supported by time-course analysis of pharynx position shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Injections of wntP-2 and ptk7 dsRNA as late as day 1 and day 2 after amputation can posteriorly shift the pharynx position.
source: Injections of wntP-2 and ptk7 dsRNA only prior to amputation, or as late as day 1 and day 2, were capable of posteriorly shifting the laminin expression domain (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by timed dsRNA delivery experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: wntP-2 expression is reduced in ndl-3(RNAi) tail fragments.
source: wntP-2 expression was reduced in ndl-3(RNAi) tail fragments, particularly along the lateral edges (Figure 6C), and posteriorly restricted in ptk7(RNAi) regenerating tail fragments (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A), suggesting that these genes can normally promote expression of wntP-2 in regenerating tail fragments.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis in ndl-3(RNAi) tail fragments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ndl-3 expression is expanded posteriorly in ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) tail fragments.
source: By contrast, ndl-3 expression was expanded posteriorly in ptk7(RNAi) and ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) tail fragments (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ptk7 and wntP-2 together suppress expression of ndl-3 in the posterior of uninjured animals.
source: We inhibited ptk7 and wntP-2 in uninjured animals to determine whether this effect was specific for regenerating tail fragments. Such animals expressed ndl-3 ectopically posterior to the pharynx at a time (by 12 days of homeostatic RNAi) prior to significant pharynx formation (Figure 6E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis in uninjured animals shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: The majority of ectopic ndl-3+ cells in ptk7(RNAi);wntP-2(RNAi) animals co-express collagen and are located within the body-wall musculature.
source: Analysis of these ectopic ndl-3+ cells by double-FISH revealed that the majority (41/63) co-expressed collagen and were located within the plane of the body-wall musculature (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by double FISH analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Ptk7 proteins encode cell-surface Wnt co-receptors with a predicted intracellular pseudokinase domain.
source: Ptk7 proteins encode cell-surface Wnt co-receptors with a predicted intracellular pseudokinase domain that participate in noncanonical, β-catenin-independent Wnt signaling (Lu et al., 2004), and can either weakly suppress or activate canonical β-catenin-dependent Wnt signaling in a context-dependent manner (Peradziryi et al., 2011; Puppo et al., 2011; Hayes et al., 2013; Bin-Nun et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from cited literature about Ptk7 protein structure and function.

claim: In mice, Ptk7 deletion causes defects in axis formation including lack of convergent extension within the trunk and tail.
source: In mice and zebrafish, Ptk7 deletion causes defects in axis formation including a lack of convergent extension within the trunk and tail and a mispolarized auditory epithelium in mice, similar to disruption of core planar cell polarity components that signal independently of beta-catenin (Lu et al., 2004; Hayes et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on cited studies of Ptk7 function in vertebrate model organisms.

claim: Planarians and most other animals have expression of multiple Wnts in posterior domains.
source: Planarians and most other animals have expression of multiple Wnts in posterior domains, pointing to their ancient use in organizing the primary body axis (Petersen and Reddien, 2009).
evidence: Based on comparative expression analysis and citation to prior work.

claim: In mammals, FGFRL1 and Wnt4 are each required for formation of the metanephric kidney from intermediate mesoderm.
source: In mammals, FGFRL1 and Wnt4 are each required for formation of the metanephric kidney from intermediate mesoderm, suggesting this positive regulatory relationship is conserved (Stark et al., 1994; Gerber et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited studies of FGFRL1 and Wnt4 function in mammalian kidney development.

claim: Graded expression of paracrine factors across fields of cells could enable patterning over large length-scales necessary for adult regeneration.
source: Graded expression of paracrine factors across fields of cells could enable patterning over the large length-scales necessary for adult regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how gradient expression could function in regeneration.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling controls anterior-versus-posterior pole identity in planarian regeneration.
source: Canonical Wnt signaling controls anterior-versus-posterior pole identity in planarian regeneration, with principal upstream determinants wnt1 expressed at the posterior pole (Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Gurley et al., 2010) and the secreted Wnt inhibitor notum expressed at the anterior pole (Petersen and Reddien, 2011), both activated transcriptionally early after wounding.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from cited prior studies of Wnt signaling in planarian regeneration.

claim: Inhibition of Wnt signaling components β-catenin-1, wnt1, Evi/wntless, Dvl-1/2 and teashirt causes regeneration of ectopic heads.
source: Inhibition of Wnt signaling components β-catenin-1, wnt1, Evi/wntless, Dvl-1/2 and teashirt causes regeneration of ectopic heads (Gurley et al., 2008; Iglesias et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Owen et al., 2015; Reuter et al., 2015); conversely, inhibition of APC or notum can cause regeneration of ectopic tails (Gurley et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple cited prior studies.

claim: Inhibition of APC or notum can cause regeneration of ectopic tails.
source: Inhibition of Wnt signaling components β-catenin-1, wnt1, Evi/wntless, Dvl-1/2 and teashirt causes regeneration of ectopic heads (Gurley et al., 2008; Iglesias et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Owen et al., 2015; Reuter et al., 2015); conversely, inhibition of APC or notum can cause regeneration of ectopic tails (Gurley et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from cited prior studies.

claim: The pharynx is formed from FoxA+ precursors derived from smedwi-1+ neoblasts.
source: The pharynx is formed from FoxA+ precursors derived from smedwi-1+ neoblasts.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of planarian pharynx development.

claim: fzd-1/2/7 encodes a predicted Wnt receptor expressed broadly.
source: fzd-1/2/7 encodes a predicted Wnt receptor expressed broadly (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by expression pattern shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and sequence homology.

claim: Co-inhibition of ptk7 with fzd-1/2/7 enhances the ectopic pharynx phenotype.
source: Co-inhibition of ptk7 with either wntP-2/wnt11-5/wnt4b (hereafter referred to as wntP-2), ndl-3, Dvl-2 (Almuedo-Castillo et al., 2011), or fzd-1/2/7 caused the strongest enhancement of the ectopic pharynx phenotype, resulting in 100% of animals affected, whereas co-inhibition with other PCGs affected this phenotype more weakly and below statistical significance under these conditions.
evidence: Supported by RNAi enhancement screen data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: fzd1/2/7 inhibition alone causes ectopic mouth and pharynx formation similar to ptk7 and/or wntP-2 inhibition.
source: We verified that RNAi of fzd1/2/7 alone resulted in ectopic mouth and pharynx formation similar to ptk7 and/or wntP-2 inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Dvl-2 but not Dvl-1 can interact with ptk7 genetically.
source: Similarly, we verified that Dvl-2 but not Dvl-1 could interact with ptk7 genetically, suggesting the involvement of Dvl-2 in trunk suppression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Inhibition of vangl1, vangl2, DAAM1 and ROCK does not increase or decrease the occurrence of ectopic mouth or pharynx phenotypes when combined with ptk7 RNAi.
source: Ptk7 proteins can act in planar cell polarization so we tested for possible functional interactions between ptk7 and components of the Planar Cell Polarity pathway vangl1, vangl2, DAAM1 and ROCK but inhibition of these genes did not increase or decrease the occurrence of ectopic mouth or pharynx phenotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.
